children.text:
Trouble is you can declare things to be true that are strictly speaking mathematically false, and from there get to proving any falsehood.

The Dirac delta function is a famous example of something mathematically non-rigorous at its inception, and mathematicians objected to it, but a few decades later Laurent Schwartz developed generalized function theory, that made it work.

Or going even further back, calculus was done in terms of ratios of infinitesimals (like dy/dx) or infinite sums of them (integrals). A century or two later the formulas of calculus were proven rigorously through classical analysis (delta-epsilon proofs) but that lost sight of the original motivations. A century or two after THAT, nonstandard analysis made a rigorous theory of infinitesimals, but reliant on relatively high powered mathematical logic that didn't exist til the 1950s or so.

Right now I think quantum field theory (renormalization, path integrals etc.) have been put on a sound mathematical basis but physicists mostly don't care. And very recently, an AI proved something about Yang-Mills theory that helped rigorize part of the Standard Model of particle physics. I don't understand that last part at all.

Besides physics, a lot of the procedures of machine learning and AI are mathematically suspicious but people use it anyway because it empirically works. People in the field have told me that yeah, they expect mathematicians will someday get around to backing it up, but for now, practitioners are moving forward with what they have.

children.author: epihelix

children.text:
Fair enough. My earliest exposure to scientific experimental work was working (on an unrelated engineering project) alongside some scientists and PhD students in an NMR lab. I got the impression that they spent the bulk of their time tinkering with the mechanical aspects of the NMR machines to set up experiments, then waiting hours while the experiments ran, and then staring at the results to figure out what to do next.

Then I had friends studying biotech who seemed to spend hours in labs slicing up flies or preparing cultures for experimental assays.

They were all definitely very smart and hard-working, and the science was extremely deep, but setting up and carrying out the experiments seemed to be the most time-consuming aspect, which may have skewed my perceptions.

> but seems to me the majority of time goes into the relatively rote work of setting up equipment, running experiments and recording the results.

Sadly, no. There are surely exceptions, but most data collection for experimental research is highly skilled and intellectually demanding.

The good RAs are the ones that could have aced a PhD if they'd wanted to (there's one in my lab, and they're worth their weight in gold) -- but they are rare. There's a reason that the majority of research effort in the sciences comes from PhD students and postdocs, not from RAs. This stuff is not simple, and definitely not rote.

I agree, and this may be nitpicking, but would it not be more accurate to say “bulk of the effort” rather than “intellectual effort”?

My perception is that most data collection, once designed (which does take considerable thought, as you point out), is a slog of executing rather mechanical processes over a long time. (Which is what RA’s and lab assistants are for!) For sure, regular analysis is needed to ensure the right data is being collected and no confounding factors are sneaking in, but seems to me the majority of time goes into the relatively rote work of setting up equipment, running experiments and recording the results.

I do think that with access to MCP-enabled equipment, AI would be ideal for this too, given its infinite patience. The problem, as with all other fields, is this would rob novices the opportunity of building the necessary intuition that comes from spending time in the weeds.
In empirical research, getting the right data represents the bulk of the intellectual effort. Designing the right experiment and collecting good data is painstaking, backbreaking work.

children.author: tomrod
children.text:
I'd argue that "the right data" should really be called "the right information in context."

Context is king.

In my (limited) experience it does not struggle with empirical research — at least in the procedural aspects thereof — as long as it has access to the right data.

It is very good at understanding research goals, identifying appropriate datasets to work with, doing data wrangling and data science, determining appropriate metrics, running simulations, analyzing results, writing up reports with charts and tables, and proposing follow ups or “high potential next steps” which show a surprising amount of judgment, and if instructed to, executing on those too.

I use Astra and Fable (who delegate to cheaper models for coding) and have them review each others work, and only spot check things when they are done calling each other out. I rarely find issues, and when I do, it’s usually a misunderstanding of intentions.

I’ve only explored a few areas though, including computer vision, vector search, and wireless signal processing, all in applications that, as far as I can tell, are genuinely novel (though of varying levels of novelty and economic value, as the models are fond of pointing out to me!)

I prefer being in the loop and setting the direction — because I do not have unlimited tokens, hah! —- and I regularly identify new directions they had not considered or had prematurely dismissed… so I am a bit more useful than just a financier of tokens! But I can totally see how they could grinding ahead by themselves and brute force useful results, especially if given very concrete goals like a theorem to prove.

I don’t think we’re at Recursive Self Improvement yet, but I don’t doubt for a minute that this is behind the insane pace of development at Anthropic and OpenAI.

Careful, the article is only a memoir, with a clear narrative arc. You should reach out to the author rather than risk reaching conclusions in a reductionist manner.

The beginning:

  My girlfriend asked me that question, after work over drinks at some shiny Manhattan bar, after another stressful day on the trading floor.
The conclusion interspersed with the author contemplating "what if" vacationing all around the US:

  [Prof Rajeev] ticked through a catalog of his contemporaries who'd succeeded in theoretical physics even without having the towering mathematical intellect that I was sure it took and that Rajeev surely has ... by focusing on problems that played to their strengths, or by taking advantage of computers, or by collaborating with peers who had complementary skills.

  ... I realized [Rajeev] sounded familiar ... he sounded a lot like me, the many times I'd been asked by young strivers how to break into Wall Street or how to succeed once there. Often I'd see my listener's eyes glaze over as I gave them such practical advice and stressed how much work it took. So many people seemed to want some secret that wasn't mine to give.

  ... Gradually, I heard what Rajeev was saying ... 'You did not fail, Bob. You quit' ... But Rajeev wasn't finished, "The hardest part of all is controlling your emotions." ... children.text: If the human is involved, "where what the human is saying to guide the model", then the prompts are even more important to include. Is this a case of "solve an open problem in theoretical physics, make no mistakes", or a case where a human had to interact frequently with the model?

I think everyone asking for this kind of thing doesn't really understand the scale and complexity of solving a big problem with many agents.

For any of the big things I've worked on, it isn't one "prompt", it's a goal that keeps getting updated and a bunch of back-and-forth steering of the model and sub agents, where what the human is saying to guide the model is heavily context dependent on what the model is currently doing or saying. Much of that guidance will ultimately be useless guidance on dead-end explorations. Also, the model will likely have written huge programs to solve things symbolically or simulate things numerically, and both the programs that were written, and the output of those programs are critical to understanding how the model came up with the things that led to a solution.

Now, I'd be all for publishing the full transcript, but the transcript is likely to be massive. Gigabytes of text, and reproducing the local computation (often sympy or numpy) may be hundreds or thousands of CPU-hours.
I think AI papers should always include prompt / prompting history as an annex

Many open problems in physics are open because we lack experimental data. No amount of numerics is going to help you. Finding a way to probe the right energy scales is  usually the obstacle, or observing enough events of something, collecting enough data, to get a statistically significant result. Either that, or the equations are so complex that numerical calculations are completely unfeasible.

In physics if you have a important open problem, you can probably just throw numerics at it to compare theory with experiment. The mathematical insight on the other hand is there to illuminate what's going on in nature, which is a much more amorphous target than the lists of very concrete problems mathematicians have just lying around.

children.author: _mjk
children.text:
Maths starts from axioms / existing proven work, and extends knowledge with newly proven facts.

Theoretical physics starts from (incomplete) observation and compatible theories plus targets an open question. There often are many solutions, but the real question is, which one holds up if the broader field is examined?

Consider what happened to the observation of the Higgs boson? There were numerous string theory flavors, all (more or less) consistent with current observations, but predicting different mass for the Higgs. Clear path for elimination of a lot of previously "correct" models.

In that empirical approach, making experiments and comparing to old/current/future work is a necessity to judge a models in a given regime. In fact, it is the differentiating factor in maths and theoretical physics.
Why is it so different in maths compared to theoretical physics?

Physicist here. I don't have time right now to read the papers in depth, nor are the results directly in my area, but I would say a few things.

One is that there are a near-infinite number of "open problems" in physics because the surface area of research programs in theoretical physics is extremely large. Before I was in the world of physics, I would have thought that "solving an open problem" meant that physicists around the world would be rejoicing and discussing the result. In reality, other than for the big, field-defining questions, only a small handful of people might care about any problem being solved. That holds true even for the Millennium problems.

Even if I were to read these papers in depth and understand them, without talking to somebody that knows the area and what has been done in it already, I would have no sense of the significance. The way to assess significance is to see how the community responds. Only time will tell whether people care about these results enough to cite them, incorporate them in future work, etc.

And so, like many other people I know, I plan to ignore all of these results until somebody I know comes and tells me to check one out: the cost of assessing any of them is too high, and there are too many other papers to read.
